title: Can You Care Too Much
author: Asha Wright
summary: In a personal essay for a leadership and wellbeing newsletter, Asha Wright describes discovering, while supporting someone close to her through a difficult stretch, that empathy has a functional ceiling she previously believed didn't exist. She traces the gradual slide from normal concern into unhealthy enmeshment: overanalyzing tone of voice, rehearsing conversations before they happen, and eventually absorbing the other person's mood as her own to the point of losing sleep. Wright connects this specifically to her self-described identity as a 'fixer' whose love language is action, arguing that the compulsion to intervene is more self-serving than it appears, since taking action creates a false sense of control over a situation that isn't actually hers to control. The piece's practical payoff is a concrete somatic exercise from her executive coach: a hand on the chest and stomach paired with three explicit reminders (I care, their journey is theirs, my wellbeing counts too) used to physically interrupt the spiral. Her closing reframe is aimed at anyone in a caregiving or leadership role: carrying someone else's pain around all day doesn't remove any of it from them, it simply produces two people having a bad day instead of one.
points: Traces a specific, gradual escalation from healthy concern into unhealthy enmeshment: overanalyzing tone of voice, rehearsing future conversations, and eventually losing sleep by absorbing another person's mood as her own.

Names herself explicitly as a 'fixer' whose love language is action, and argues the compulsion to intervene is more self-serving than altruistic, since taking action manufactures a false sense of control over what isn't actually controllable.

Reframes worry itself as a self-deceiving substitute for care, arguing that carrying someone else's pain all day doesn't remove any of it from them, it just produces two people having a bad day instead of one.

Supplies a specific, repeatable somatic technique from her executive coach (hand on chest, hand on stomach, slowed breathing, three verbal reminders) as a physical interrupt for over-identification with someone else's emotional state.

Closes with a reframe applicable beyond personal relationships to any caregiving or leadership role: knowing where another person's feelings end and your own begin doesn't reduce how much you care, it improves your actual capacity to help.
quotes: I always thought empathy could never be excessive. Over recent months I've been forced to rethink my position and I've started questioning where empathy has a functional ceiling.
Eventually, without me realising, their mood became mine and I found it impossible to separate the two. That's when I had to be honest with myself about where I'd landed.
I'm a fixer, and always have been. My love language is action, meaning the way I express that I care for someone is doing something for them. The trouble is people don't behave like problems.

Somewhere along the way I'd started treating worry as proof that I cared, but carrying someone else's pain around all day doesn't take any of it off them. It just means two people are having a bad day instead of one, and that helps nobody.
Sometimes loving someone means knowing where their feelings end and yours begin. That distinction doesn't make you care less. It puts you in a better position to truly help.
